core: Dynamics as musical loudness and softness
Amplitude as a sound-wave property related to volume
Relative dynamic levels and gradual changes such as crescendo and decrescendo
supporting: Listening for dynamic contrast and change within an excerpt
Distinguishing dynamics from tempo, timbre, texture, pitch, and articulation
Separating a description of loudness from an unsupported claim about meaning or quality
outOfScope: Sound-level measurement, hearing safety, or acoustical engineering advice
A complete catalog of Western notation and performance conventions
Claims that loud or soft music has a universal emotional meaning

claims.claim: Dynamics concern the volume or loudness and softness of musical sound; in the sound-wave account used by the LOUIS text, volume corresponds with amplitude.
Dynamics can be described as loud, soft, medium, gradually louder, or gradually softer; crescendo and decrescendo are labels for gradual change in loudness.
Dynamics are distinct from tempo, which concerns speed, and from timbre, which concerns tone color or quality.
A change in loudness can occur without a change in musical texture, melody, or instrumentation, so listeners should report the changed element precisely.
Dynamic observations are most reliable when made comparatively within an excerpt, for example by identifying which entrance is softer, louder, or gradually changing.
A loudness observation does not by itself establish a single emotional meaning, musical value, or performer intention.
